data.name: Scott in Space
data.detailed_description:
Picture this. One guniea pig alone in the vastness of space, fighting an empire of evil Rhinos. Sure, that's pretty unfair...the Rhinos don't stand a chance!

Scott in Space is a stylized platformer with a classic gameplay core, plenty of different enemies to defeat and quests to fulfill. Can you stop the evil Rhino Empire from abducting guinea pigs from their home world New New Guinea? Can you defeat the dark rhino leader named... Evil Andy?! Can you make it home before dinner? So many questions and so little time!



If you like the light-weight sphere of classic family platformers and you love helping little guinea pigs in space out from time to time (an uncommon hobby), then Scott in Space is the right game for you!



While the easier difficulty modes satisfy beginners and casual players, the hard and the evil difficutly mode confidently challenge hardcore players.

Scott in Space is the debut indie title developed by Ragiva Games. The design team of this game is a group of three indie devs with experience from the games industry who decided to go their own way.

FEATURES


- Prove your guniea pig platformer skills (you have them, right?)
- Fulfill quests for questionable characters
- Enjoy a dead-serious story with non-existent rodent-rhino war humor
- Explore over 50 levels across 7 planets
- Sing along to the orchestral soundtrack (or just listen while playing, your call!)

reviews.review:
Scott in Space is a quirky 2D action platformer that takes a deliberately absurd idea and turns it into a colorful interplanetary adventure. Instead of relying on a conventional science-fiction hero, the game puts a guinea pig at the center of a conflict involving an aggressive empire of rhinos. Developed by Ragiva Games e.K., which is also the primary company associated with publishing the game, it embraces the personality of a small independent production. Its strongest qualities come from its humorous setting, accessible platforming, and willingness to build an entire adventure around an intentionally ridiculous premise.

The story follows Scott as he travels through space after the Rhino Empire begins abducting guinea pigs from their home planet of New New Guinea. His journey ultimately places him in opposition to Evil Andy and an assortment of hostile creatures and unusual personalities. The narrative is intentionally playful rather than dramatic, using strange characters, humorous dialogue, and exaggerated situations to give the campaign some personality. Quests obtained along the way provide additional objectives and help make the journey feel like more than a simple sequence of disconnected platforming stages.

Gameplay follows familiar side-scrolling platform conventions. Scott must navigate environments filled with enemies, obstacles, platforms, and other hazards while progressing toward objectives. There are more than 50 levels distributed across seven planets, giving the adventure a reasonable amount of content and allowing the scenery and challenges to change as the campaign progresses. The mechanics remain relatively straightforward, making the game easy to understand without lengthy tutorials or complicated systems. Anyone familiar with traditional platform games should quickly understand its basic rhythm of movement, jumping, avoiding danger, and dealing with enemies.

One of the more welcome design decisions is the inclusion of multiple difficulty settings. Players primarily interested in seeing the different planets and following the humorous story can select an easier experience, while Hard and Evil settings provide additional challenge. This flexibility makes the game suitable for different skill levels and offers an incentive to replay stages after completing the campaign. Higher difficulties can make otherwise familiar encounters more demanding, although the underlying gameplay remains fundamentally traditional regardless of the selected setting.

Visually, the game uses a colorful cartoon-like presentation that suits its unusual premise. A realistic visual direction would hardly complement a story about guinea pigs fighting an empire of rhinos, so the exaggerated art style feels appropriate. The planets and characters help reinforce the lighthearted atmosphere, even though the graphical detail and animation naturally reflect the limitations of a smaller indie production. The orchestral soundtrack is a particularly interesting touch, giving portions of the adventure a larger sense of scale than might be expected from its modest presentation.

There are limitations that become more noticeable over longer sessions. The platforming does not possess the mechanical depth or exceptionally refined movement found in the strongest representatives of the genre. Players expecting elaborate abilities, extensive character development, complex exploration systems, or highly innovative level mechanics may find the experience fairly basic. Its humor is similarly dependent on personal taste. The strange premise provides plenty of personality, but players who do not enjoy deliberately silly comedy may not find the story especially engaging.

The modest technical demands are beneficial for anyone using an older or less powerful computer. The game was designed around relatively lightweight hardware requirements and occupies little storage space compared with modern releases. This simplicity fits the overall design philosophy: it is an uncomplicated single-player platforming experience intended to be easy to start and understand rather than a technically demanding production.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently best regarded as Unverified rather than officially confirmed as Verified or Playable. The lightweight nature of the game suggests that raw hardware performance should not be a major concern, but an absence of an official compatibility rating means players should not assume a completely trouble-free handheld experience. Controls, display behavior, launcher requirements, or other compatibility details may require individual testing.

Scott in Space ultimately works best for players who appreciate unusual indie games and uncomplicated platforming. Its combination of more than 50 stages, seven planets, selectable difficulty levels, quests, cartoon presentation, orchestral music, and bizarre science-fiction comedy gives it more character than its simple mechanics initially suggest. It lacks the refinement and mechanical sophistication needed to compete with the best modern platformers, but its cheerful personality and peculiar concept make it memorable enough for genre fans willing to accept some rough edges. 

Rating: 6/10
